cells.tense: You are here at the work, learning what grows by tending it, and you know it.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you are tending and show it to somebody this week, just as it is, unfinished.
cells.core:
You're the one with your hands in it, learning what grows by tending it. You don't need the outcome already fixed to keep showing up, and that is the whole trick — attention first, results later. What you've been feeding is coming up, and you can see it coming up.

The proof is right in front of you, which is why it's easy to miss. When something is finished and you can let it go without having to hold on, that letting go is how the work completes. Growth here doesn't leave you emptied out. It leaves you free to feed the next thing.
cells.sheetLine: You learn what grows by tending it, and you can let it go when it's done.
cells.place: in the garden where things are coming up

cells.tense: You are bracing for a harvest that hasn't been planted yet, and pushing it to arrive.
cells.ask: Set down the thing you keep checking on, leave it for three days, and take up one unrelated thing that only needs your attention.
cells.core:
You're spending today on a crop that hasn't been planted. Every check, every adjustment, is you trying to reach a future where it's already fine — and that future keeps not arriving, so the work keeps not ending. You're forcing the growth instead of tending it.

What you're out for is growth that doesn't need forcing — care that leaves you with something left over. The better move is to quit reaching for the far end and put your hands on what's here right now, even something small. When you can let one thing be unfinished without hovering over it, the care stops costing you so much.
cells.sheetLine: You're pushing growth that can't be rushed. Let it be unfinished for a day.
cells.place: in the garden where things are coming up

cells.tense: Your hands are not in the work, and you are standing outside it watching instead.
cells.ask: Pick one small living thing or growing project and do one thing for it — water it, arrange it, read one page about it — without deciding it has to matter.
cells.core:
You know how to tend things. The doing of it, though, isn't happening. The reach that used to go out and touch something living isn't going out, and you stay at the edge while the work goes on without you. The skill is still there. The offering isn't.

Patience and knowledge aren't what's short here. The part of you that finishes something and is seen doing it hasn't been fed. Don't try to force the care back on. Feed the other side — the confidence that comes from finishing one small thing and being glad of it. One thing done with your own hands, and the current comes back through.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped handing it over. Pick one small living thing and tend it once.
cells.place: in the garden where things are coming up

cells.tense: You're already tending what's growing, but you'd say you're just keeping things going.
cells.ask: Catch yourself in one moment of tending this week and tell someone that this was your care, not just upkeep.
cells.core:
You're already doing the work. You're the one watering it, moving it into the light, learning what it needs at each stage of coming up. You call it logistics, or just getting through the week. The caring is real and it's running. What's absent is only your own say-so about it.

Picture this working: something finishes, and you let it go on purpose, glad of it instead of gripped by it. Then you say, out loud, that the care was yours. That last part isn't happening yet. One honest moment of naming it — this is mine, my hands did this — is enough to start. An unclaimed thing stays half-finished, however well it grows.
cells.sheetLine: You call it maintenance. The care is yours, and you can name it.
cells.place: in the garden where things are coming up

attempts.check: The unsupported claim I had to cut was that the person has been through a specific loss of a garden or a growing thing that made them stop tending — the record says nothing about what happened, only that the offering stopped. A reader could reasonably say 'I am still right here in it, not behind a door,' so Too Little must describe the capacity being withdrawn, not the person being gone. The ask survives being wrong: noticing what's already sprouting and naming the next small thing to do with your hands teaches something about attention even if the diagnosis misses. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line that praises their patience as a virtue, so it is gone.
